This is therefore the first time that we have presented a complete edition of this correspondence, at least without the spirit of censorship. It consists of two hundred and sixty-three sheets, archived without the slightest chronological concern, the majority of which has been numbered from 99 to 318.

In total, there are one hundred and ninety-four letters and notes from Isabelle and a single letter from Marie-Christine which is a portrait of her correspondent. The whole thing extends over a period of more than three years: from July 1760 to November 1763. The difficulties inherent in this manuscript are of different orders.

First, Isabelle de Bourbon-Parma, who speaks four languages, uses French and German here, but often with inappropriate expressions. Although the vast majority of letters are written in French, they are often peppered with Germanisms and incorrections. Furthermore, as was common at that time, she ignored the art of punctuation. All things which do not make it easy to understand.

We therefore chose to modernize the spelling as well as establish the punctuation. A small minority of letters and notes (sometimes written in tiny handwriting on very small pieces of paper) in German from the 16th century were translated almost literally and printed in italics to better distinguish them from French.

Water, stains or ink stains make certain words or groups of words completely illegible. In this case, we indicate it with a note. But the major problem with this correspondence is above all of a chronological order. The vast majority of letters are undated. This absence of dating is the source of inevitable errors on our part.

For example, she will compare the Archduke to him in this eternal boredom in which he is immersed, in his jealousy, etc. To condemn him is good for the moment, but if it comes back to her mind at another moment, it is to do herself a disservice to her forever. To approve of it is to believe oneself wiser than it.
